[ReZero](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v161/bachlechner21a/bachlechner21a.pdf) initializes residual gates at zero, making each block an identity with identity input Jacobian. For z=h+αr and g=∂L/∂z, chain rule gives ∂L/∂α=gᵀr and a branch-only parameter gradient α(∂r/∂θ)ᵀg. Thus the gate can learn immediately; branch-only parameters initially receive zero task gradient through that branch. This establishes initial signal propagation, not guaranteed stability throughout training or improved recommendation accuracy.

Placement matters: h+αr(LN(h)) preserves the identity at α=0; LN(h+αr) instead starts at LN(h), with its normalization Jacobian. Adding a residual before an existing final LN preserves that baseline at zero, but adding it afterward is a different extension. [Pre-LN analysis](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/xiong20b.html) establishes better-behaved initialization gradients under its Transformer assumptions; ReZero’s Transformer experiments remove LayerNorm. [Fixup](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.09321) additionally uses depth-dependent branch initialization to control functional updates: a zero initial branch alone does not establish subsequent scale stability.

For already-trained, shared input/output embeddings, the applicable conclusions are algebraic: zero α preserves the baseline forward computation, and blocks only the new branch’s gradient contribution. Embeddings still receive gradients through the existing encoder and tied output scorer. This is an extension of a trained model, not ReZero initialization of the whole network. Scale is consequential: under plain SGD, replacing r by cr multiplies the initial gate gradient by c and the first residual contribution by c². Tied logits gain αEr, making embedding norms relevant too. These deductions do not inherit the papers’ training guarantees. Reproducibility requires specifying residual placement, embedding scaling, normalization, gate optimizer settings, and monitoring |α|‖r‖/‖h‖ and logit changes.
